parsed.attack: UK/EU law already forces allergens to be emphasised in bold inside the ingredients list, so the manual check this replaces is a two-second glance that is free, trusted and already habitual - the wedge promises two seconds against an incumbent that is also two seconds. Worse, no parent of a child with a confirmed anaphylactic allergy will accept an offline model's yes/no as the final word; they will scan and then read the panel anyway, so the app adds a step rather than removing one, and the residual real pain ('may contain traces') is a precautionary statement OCR cannot adjudicate. Behaviourally, lunchbox shopping converges on a fixed repertoire of about twenty safe SKUs within weeks, which is exactly why the author's own first kill metric - a second scan within seven days - is the one that will fire. The demand evidence offered is zero observed parent behaviour: the pain paragraph is an assertion about the unit economics of grocery delivery, and the only citation is a different product that failed.
parsed.strongest_defence: The acute case is not the familiar weekly basket but the unfamiliar packet - imported own-brand items, long ingredient lists, school-fete and holiday buying - and the value sold is not time saved but a second check that converts a moment of anxiety into a decision; anxiety products around a child's safety convert at rates that everyday utilities never reach, and the persistent avoid-list (not the OCR) is what compounds.
parsed.verdict_reason: The pain is real but already discharged by mandated bold-allergen labelling and a fixed shopping repertoire, leaving a narrow anxiety-purchase niche rather than a recurring job.
